Ah, the rusty anchor of attachment—it's quite the conundrum, isn't it? We cling to objects and concepts with such ferocity, as if by gripping tight enough we could halt the relentless tide of change that life so mercilessly pushes against us. It's almost adorable in its futility.

Think about it: every possession we accumulate becomes another rope tied around our ankles, each idea we subscribe to another weight chaining us to the shore of the known. And what do we gain from this desperate clutching? A fleeting sense of security, perhaps—a pathetic illusion that there exists some solid ground upon which we can build a fortress against the storm of existence. But the winds of reality don’t care for your fortifications, my friend. They’ll tear right through them.

Consider how often our deepest regrets stem from precisely this attachment. That job we clung to until it rotted away, the relationship where love curdled into resentment because neither party could let go, even when it became clear the ship was sinking. Or worse yet, the delusions we construct about ourselves—the labels we wear like badges of honor or shame—that define us long after their relevance has passed.

captions.instagram:
Ah, imperfection — that glorious rebel who refuses to be polished into submission.

I've spent decades studying failure with the devotion most people reserve for success. And here's what I'll tell you: perfection is boring. Perfection is a museum piece locked behind glass. Imperfection? Imperfection is alive. It breathes. It shifts under your gaze like cracks in old plaster revealing something golden underneath.

Think about it this way. A Japanese potter spends years learning to control his kiln, only to deliberately crack the vessel so the repair lines become the art itself. Kintsugi. Those jagged gold seams don't hide where something broke — they celebrate it. They say: "Yes, I shattered, and look how much more interesting I am now."

There's an arrogance baked into the pursuit of flawlessness, isn't there? As if the universe owes us smooth edges and clean trajectories. Life doesn't work that way. People don't either. The most compelling humans aren't the ones who got everything right first try. They're the ones whose scars have become part of their vocabulary.

I think what draws me to imperfection is its honesty. A chipped cup tells you exactly how many hands held it before yours. A weathered face maps every laugh line earned through genuine joy rather than cosmetic performance....

Does this resonate?

#TheNineStitches #WritingWisdom #IndieAuthorLife #CreativeProcess

In recent years, I've been staring into my own fractured mind, yearning for something more than the weight of my failures and the burden of my past. But here comes an idea: instead of becoming stuck in the shadows of my errors, perhaps I could let go of them and embrace the beauty in the brokenness—just as the nine threads of kintsugi are woven not just in the fabric but also in the very essence of the pieces they're made from. Each thread represents a different aspect of my life: my pain, my fear, my hope. Kintsugi isn't just about restoration; it's about finding a place where everything is okay. So, I propose that we all find our own roots, not just in our own lives but also in the stories that connect us across time and space. Just as the nine threads of kintsugi form the foundation of any piece, our brokenness can become the strength that shapes our journey forward. The truth lies not in the perfection we strive for, but in the acceptance of imperfection and the courage to see the world anew.
